# Golf MK4 Turn Signals Not Working While Hazards Function

A common electrical anomaly in the Volkswagen Golf MK4 involves a scenario where the turn signals appear completely dead upon startup, yet the hazard lights function perfectly. The user observed that after parking for only 10 to 15 minutes, the system behaved differently than when driving all day. This discrepancy immediately points to a specific circuit topology rather than a general power failure.

The core of this issue lies in how the turn signal and hazard flasher modules are wired within the MK4's architecture. In many vehicles of this era, the turn signals do not have their own dedicated power source; instead, they draw voltage from the hazard switch. The hazard lights are essentially hardwired directly to the battery through a fuse, while the left and right turn signal circuits pass through the hazard switch before reaching the flasher relay.

Because the hazards work perfectly, you can eliminate the main fuse for that circuit as the culprit. If the primary fuse were blown or corroded, neither the hazards nor the turn signals would illuminate. The fact that one function works while the other fails confirms that power is reaching the flasher unit and the bulbs are intact.

The logic dictates that if the hazard switch is closed (hazard lights on), it bypasses the internal contacts of the switch for the individual left/right sides, feeding full voltage to both flashers simultaneously. When you attempt to signal left or right without the hazards engaged, the circuit relies entirely on the specific contact points inside the hazard switch to complete the loop to ground.

If the turn signals fail immediately after parking and starting the car, but work when the engine is hot or after driving, thermal expansion of components should be considered. However, in this specific MK4 configuration, a more likely mechanical failure involves the internal contacts of the hazard switch itself. Over time, the plastic housing can degrade, or the metal contacts inside the switch can oxidize or melt due to heat buildup from the flasher relay.

When you park for 10â15 minutes, the components cool down slightly, but the specific contact point responsible for routing voltage to the left turn signal may be open. Interestingly, driving all day often generates enough heat in the engine bay and switchbox to temporarily expand these contacts or melt residual debris, restoring functionality only until the system cools again. This explains why the car works perfectly during a drive but fails upon returning to a cool cabin after a short stop.

To verify this without disassembling the entire dash, you can perform a continuity check using a multimeter. With the hazard switch turned off, measure resistance between the turn signal output terminals of the switch. If the reading indicates an open circuit on one side but not the other, the internal switch mechanism is faulty. Since the hazards bypass this specific path by closing both sides simultaneously, they remain functional despite the degraded left or right contact.

Replacing the hazard switch assembly is the standard resolution. It is a relatively inexpensive part for the Golf MK4 community. While some might suggest cleaning the contacts, the plastic actuator often cracks under stress, leading to intermittent failures that cleaning cannot fix.
